frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over gas exports, but European buyers are pressing for favorable pricing and long-term access as they diversify away from Russian supply.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya threatens border security and could disrupt energy infrastructure while increasing pressure for foreign security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: External control of oil value chains
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal sovereignty over petroleum resources but remains heavily dependent on foreign operators, imported technology, and external finance for production and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor strategic contest
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is attracting US, European, and Chinese interest because of its links to Congolese and Zambian minerals, creating leverage but also intensifying competition over infrastructure access.

frictionVectors.title: Niger pipeline dispute
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain strained over oil exports through Benin, exposing Cotonou to transit risks and political pressure from neighboring military governments.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and regional port competition support growth, but reliance on external capital limits Benin's control over logistics and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond market exposure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana exercises unusually strong control through its state partnership with De Beers, but weaker global diamond demand could reduce fiscal room and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals is increasing, bringing investment opportunities alongside pressure to offer concessions and infrastructure access to foreign firms.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking a larger state role in gold production and tighter oversight of foreign operators, but weak institutions and informal extraction complicate enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Expanded security ties with Russia reduce reliance on former Western partners but may exchange one form of external dependence for another while increasing sanctions and reputational risks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral licensing
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control over nickel, rare-earth and gold projects, but limited capital and regulatory capacity leave room for opaque foreign-linked concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-DRC security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions around eastern DRC and cross-border armed networks complicate trade routes and reduce Burundi's leverage over regional infrastructure and mineral corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed port infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of ports, logistics and maritime-security facilities brings investment and strategic value, but also increases dependence on external financiers and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and energy exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to external tourism demand, imported fuel and climate shocks, limiting domestic control over critical revenue and energy systems.

highlights: Ports and pipelines are strategic chokepoints

frictionVectors.title: Oil, gas and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain central to hydrocarbon and mining development, while governance weaknesses and opaque contracting limit Cameroon's ability to capture full sovereign value.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-linked infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone conflict and instability near the Far North threaten transport corridors, plantations and energy infrastructure, increasing reliance on external finance and security support.

frictionVectors.title: Russian-linked security and mining
frictionVectors.details: The government's security relationship with Russian-linked forces has expanded its room for maneuver but is associated with opaque access to gold and diamond resources.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Weak control over borderlands and transport routes leaves mineral exports dependent on neighboring states and armed-group dynamics, sharply limiting effective sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal position remains tied to oil production, export infrastructure and foreign operators, constraining domestic control over pricing, technology and revenue stability.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external security ties
frictionVectors.details: The government is balancing relations with France, Russia-linked actors and regional partners as it manages border threats, creating leverage for outsiders over strategic infrastructure and policy.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains effective control of Mayotte, limiting Comoros' territorial claims and access to surrounding maritime resources. The dispute continues to shape migration, security, and diplomatic relations.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence and fisheries oversight
frictionVectors.details: Limited enforcement capacity leaves Comorian waters vulnerable to foreign fishing and informal exploitation. Budget support and infrastructure finance from external partners constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-linked mineral networks
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border trading networks continue to challenge Kinshasa's control over mineral-rich areas in the east. Rwanda-related tensions and regional security operations complicate efforts to formalize supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in copper and cobalt production, while Western actors seek diversified access to critical minerals. The government has greater leverage than before but still struggles to capture value through processing and transparent contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil operators and volatile prices continue to shape state revenues, limiting diversification and bargaining autonomy. Production and fiscal management remain central points of external influence.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a major role in roads, public works, and commercial infrastructure. These ties deliver strategic assets but raise concerns over debt exposure, contract transparency, and domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: External capital concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment remains central to ports, energy, mining, and transport expansion, giving international firms substantial influence over strategic infrastructure. Abidjan is mitigating this through regional integration and stronger domestic institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in the Sahel continue to pressure border regions and transport corridors. Security spending and reliance on regional and international partners could constrain fiscal and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign base dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti leverages its position near the Bab el-Mandeb to host major foreign military facilities, but the resulting revenue model makes sovereignty dependent on external security patrons. Rival powers' presence increases diplomatic exposure and escalation risk.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed port and logistics projects remain central to Djibouti's development strategy and debt profile. Competition with neighboring Somaliland and Ethiopia adds pressure over corridor access, concessions, and control of critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and IMF-linked reforms increase the influence of Gulf investors and international lenders over strategic assets, ports, and state-owned enterprises.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and instability around the Red Sea threaten Suez revenues, while the GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains an unresolved constraint on long-term water security.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon decline
frictionVectors.details: Maturing oil fields and weak diversification reduce fiscal room, increasing dependence on foreign technical partners and opaque production-sharing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: China-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Major infrastructure ties with Chinese contractors provide strategic capacity but also leave the state exposed to concentrated external financing and repayment risks.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb attract competing regional and international security interests, limiting Asmara's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining partnerships provide scarce export revenue but create pressure over transparency, labor practices, and the distribution of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Economic dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, customs revenue, energy, and transport links remain heavily tied to South Africa, leaving Eswatini vulnerable to external economic conditions and policy spillovers.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy pressure
frictionVectors.details: Political restrictions and periodic unrest complicate efforts to attract diversified investment beyond sugar, textiles, and South African-linked supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD increases Ethiopia's control over electricity generation but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan over dam operations and downstream water security.

frictionVectors.title: Port-access vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: As a landlocked state, Ethiopia depends on external corridors, especially through Djibouti, while tensions involving Somaliland and regional actors complicate efforts to diversify maritime access.

highlights: Oil and manganese remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractives
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is seeking greater state participation and local value addition in oil and manganese, but Chinese, French and other foreign firms remain central to financing, operations and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Resource exports depend heavily on the Owendo port and the Transgabon railway, leaving national revenue vulnerable to infrastructure bottlenecks and external project financing.

highlights: Fishing and tourism face external pressure

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for surrounding-market access, transport corridors and energy connectivity, limiting policy autonomy despite formal sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign fleets and weak monitoring threaten coastal livelihoods and food security, while licensing revenues remain difficult to capture transparently.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated small-scale gold mining is damaging watersheds and agricultural land, while political and commercial networks complicate enforcement and formalization.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is attracting external interest in lithium, bauxite and manganese, but fiscal constraints and investor-led project structures could limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridor dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou rail-and-port system and major bauxite operations are financed and operated through large foreign consortia, creating leverage over Guinea's export routes and fiscal receipts.

frictionVectors.title: Junta legitimacy and contract risk
frictionVectors.details: The military government is using mining projects to secure revenue and legitimacy, but opaque renegotiations and political uncertainty raise concerns over sovereignty, labor rights and long-term state control.

frictionVectors.title: Transnational narcotics networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and porous maritime borders leave Guinea-Bissau exposed to cocaine trafficking networks, which can distort politics and undermine control of ports and customs.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized infrastructure and fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and foreign fishing activity provide essential capacity and revenue, but limited oversight weakens domestic bargaining power and local economic benefits.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Kenya balances IMF-linked fiscal reforms with significant Chinese and other foreign financing obligations. Debt-service pressures constrain domestic control over infrastructure and public spending priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa remains strategically important for East African trade, while competition from Tanzania and instability along regional corridors challenge Kenya's leverage over transit infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water revenues and dam construction provide vital income, but the project deepens Lesotho's dependence on South African financing, markets, and infrastructure arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Maseru's economic vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on South African trade, remittances, and supply chains limits policy autonomy and leaves Lesotho exposed to decisions made outside its borders.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-led mining operations dominate export prospects, while the government faces pressure to secure better local processing, revenue collection, and community benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor concessions
frictionVectors.details: Control of Monrovia-area logistics and mining corridors is central to Liberia's resource security, with foreign operators retaining substantial influence over infrastructure and trade flows.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks can disrupt fields, ports, and export terminals, preventing a unified national authority from exercising reliable control over hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and commercial influence
frictionVectors.details: External actors support competing Libyan power centers and seek leverage over energy, reconstruction, and security arrangements, limiting Libya's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining projects provide export earnings but leave Madagascar exposed to external ownership, commodity-price swings, and disputes over taxation and environmental costs.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and transport bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power and weak roads constrain domestic processing, reinforcing reliance on foreign capital and imported infrastructure for resource extraction and export.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi's debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages limit policy autonomy, while roads, energy, and agricultural financing remain reliant on external lenders and donors.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and mining leverage
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages and prospective uranium and rare-earth projects create openings for foreign investors, with limited domestic capacity to capture value or enforce stringent local-content rules.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking larger state stakes, tax revenues, and local processing from multinational gold producers, increasing confrontation risk with foreign mining companies.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support has displaced Western influence but has not resolved insurgency, while insecurity threatens transport corridors and mining operations.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas project exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania offshore gas project offers major export leverage but leaves Nouakchott exposed to partner coordination, revenue-sharing disputes, and foreign operator control.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports and proposed green-hydrogen projects depend on port, rail, and transmission infrastructure financed or operated with substantial outside participation.

frictionVectors.title: Diego Garcia settlement
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations over the strategic Diego Garcia base and the terms of any long-term foreign military presence.

frictionVectors.title: External economic exposure
frictionVectors.details: The island's finance, tourism, food, and fuel systems remain sensitive to global market shifts and dependence on external shipping and investment networks.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates, fisheries, ports, and renewable projects in Western Sahara generate diplomatic and legal friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some international stakeholders.

frictionVectors.title: External capital and water stress
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is building domestic value chains in automotive, aerospace, fertilizers, and renewables, but major projects still rely on European, Gulf, and Chinese capital amid severe water constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten LNG infrastructure and local sovereignty, despite support from regional and foreign security forces. Project security remains heavily dependent on outside partners.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gas, graphite, and other mineral projects rely on foreign operators and financing, limiting domestic value capture and increasing exposure to contract disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy Investment
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen, oil, and renewable projects could strengthen state revenues but remain dependent on European, Chinese, and Gulf capital, technology, and offtake markets.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Grid Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Limited water supplies, transmission capacity, and port logistics constrain efforts to convert resource wealth into domestically controlled industrial growth.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Disputes with Former Partners
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater control over uranium and other extractive assets, creating legal and operational friction with foreign companies and potential export disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from Western military partnerships has increased reliance on alternative security providers while insurgent groups continue to pressure transport corridors and state infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Control and Theft
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline sabotage, crude theft, and aging infrastructure undermine national control over petroleum revenues and keep production dependent on foreign operators and technical capital.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Gas Supply Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and weak gas-processing infrastructure limit industrial sovereignty, while pricing reforms continue to generate domestic political friction.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Linked Mineral Allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional supply chains, particularly for minerals associated with eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, remains a major source of diplomatic and sanctions risk.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Strong state coordination improves control over domestic resources, but the economy remains exposed to donor financing, foreign export markets, and regional security backlash.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest remains significant, but commercial discoveries and state revenue are still uncertain. Limited administrative capacity increases reliance on foreign operators and external technical support.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic External Competition
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, and other partners compete for influence through infrastructure, finance, and maritime cooperation. São Tomé seeks to preserve flexibility while avoiding excessive dependence on any single sponsor.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Contract Review
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national participation and transparency in offshore oil and gas projects operated with international companies. Renegotiation risks investor uncertainty and delays in revenue realization.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project requires close coordination over cross-border production, local-content rules, and revenue sharing. External operators retain major technical and financial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Tuna Fleet Access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies heavily on foreign fishing fleets and access fees, creating tension between immediate fiscal needs and long-term control of marine resources. Monitoring and enforcement capacity remain limited across its vast maritime zone.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, France, and other partners seek access and influence through port, surveillance, and maritime-security cooperation. Victoria is balancing these relationships to avoid strategic overdependence.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, gold, and emerging critical-mineral projects remain dominated by foreign capital and operators. Weak fiscal and regulatory capacity limits Sierra Leone's ability to secure durable value addition and predictable public revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure-Mining Linkages
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms are prominent in mining, construction, and related infrastructure, creating leverage through integrated financing and logistics arrangements. The government is attempting to improve local content and transparency without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led Offshore Oil Development
frictionVectors.details: Turkey and other external partners are positioned to provide exploration, security, and technical support in Somalia's offshore sector. Federal-state disputes and weak regulatory institutions could leave the country with limited control over future rents.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Somaliland Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Competition involving Ethiopia, Somaliland, Turkey, Gulf states, and other regional actors continues to shape access to ports and maritime infrastructure. These rivalries complicate Somalia's territorial claims and divert resources from domestic institution-building.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL VALUE-CHAIN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing of platinum-group metals, manganese and rare minerals while balancing Chinese, Western and Gulf investment. Policy uncertainty and weak infrastructure limit Pretoria's leverage over downstream value chains.

frictionVectors.title: GRID AND PORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and port inefficiency continue to constrain sovereign economic capacity. Private-sector participation and foreign financing are expanding, but implementation remains politically contested.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE DEPENDENCE THROUGH SUDAN
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's export oil must transit conflict-affected Sudan, leaving production, revenue and basic fiscal stability exposed to pipeline outages and rival external actors. Chinese-linked oil interests remain important, while Juba has limited bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: ARMS, SECURITY AND RESOURCE RENT-SEEKING
frictionVectors.details: Elite competition over oil revenues and security patronage continues to weaken state institutions. Regional mediation and foreign security relationships can stabilize corridors but also reinforce fragmented sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND WAR ECONOMIES
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling networks provide financing to armed actors and create openings for foreign commercial and political sponsors. The state has limited ability to regulate extraction or capture revenues transparently.

frictionVectors.title: PORT, PIPELINE AND HUMANITARIAN ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Control of transport corridors, Port Sudan and oil infrastructure is contested amid the civil war. External diplomatic, military and logistical involvement increasingly shapes access to strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Ports and LNG define strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG PROJECT SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is advancing negotiations to monetize offshore gas while seeking stronger domestic benefits and regulatory control. Delays, fiscal disputes and investor demands remain the main risks to sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: PORT CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam's role in serving landlocked neighbors attracts Gulf, Chinese and Western-linked infrastructure interest. The government is using this competition to expand capacity while guarding against excessive dependence on any single partner.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains central to Togo's revenue and regional trade strategy, with foreign operators and financiers retaining substantial influence over logistics infrastructure. This supports growth but constrains full national control of strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE AND SECURITY PRESSURES
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate remains a core sovereign resource, yet financing, technology and management constraints limit domestic value addition. Spillover insecurity from the Sahel also raises dependence on external security cooperation and threatens northern transport links.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains closely tied to migration control, giving Brussels substantial influence over Tunisian policy. Domestic opposition to externally conditioned assistance is rising amid economic stagnation.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and phosphate vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and weak phosphate production, limiting fiscal autonomy. Foreign investment is needed for infrastructure, but constrained public finances reduce negotiating power.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains strategically important but faces sustained criticism from environmental groups, Western institutions, and some financiers. Chinese and Gulf-linked capital helps preserve momentum while increasing external influence over the project.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Uganda is courting foreign partners for minerals, transport, and energy infrastructure, balancing Chinese commercial engagement against Western governance concerns. Limited domestic processing keeps much of the value chain externally controlled.

frictionVectors.title: Copper ownership and value-addition contest
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is seeking greater domestic processing and revenue capture from copper while competing Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors pursue long-term mining positions. Power shortages and transport bottlenecks weaken Zambia's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt relief and IMF-linked reforms have improved fiscal room but continue to constrain public investment and industrial policy. Creditors and mining investors retain significant influence over the pace and terms of resource-sector reform.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in lithium and other mineral projects, while Western and regional investors seek access to Zimbabwe's resource base. Weak local processing and regulatory uncertainty limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, currency, and infrastructure pressure
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions and restricted financial access complicate investment, payments, and infrastructure renewal, increasing dependence on non-Western partners. Persistent currency instability further reduces the state's ability to negotiate stable, long-term resource contracts.
